title: The Hand Still Leads: Inside the Studios Training Machines on Their Own Sketchbooks
deck: In three studios across Europe, artists build small private models from their own drawings, then overrule them. The results look nothing like the internet's idea of AI art.
author: Mara Okonkwo-Lind
disclosure: Reporting and writing by the author. Studio photographs unedited. No generative tools were used in writing this article.
hero: lead photo — Sanne Vos drawing over a printed model proposal
caption: Sanne Vos works over a faint print of a model proposal in her Rotterdam studio. Most mornings she rejects every one.
authorBio: Writes about studio practice and the tools artists build for themselves. Previously technical lead at a print workshop in Bergen.

blocks.text: Every morning at nine, before the studio fills, Sanne Vos draws for forty minutes with a 2B pencil. She has done this for nineteen years. For the last two, the drawings have gone somewhere new: into a small model, trained only on her sketchbooks, that runs on a laptop with the Wi-Fi switched off.

"It's a mirror with bad manners," she says. The model proposes compositions in her hand: the same lazy diagonals, the same habit of leaving the left edge unfinished. Most mornings she rejects all of them. Some mornings one proposal shows her a habit she didn't know she had, and she spends the afternoon breaking it.

Vos is one of a growing number of artists who treat machine learning less as a generator and more as an instrument with a narrow range. They build small, private systems, train them on their own work, and keep the final decision for themselves. The work that comes out is slower and stranger than most of what circulates online. It also, they argue, belongs to them.

The studios we visited share one technical choice: scale down. Rather than prompting a general model trained on billions of images, they fine-tune compact models on a few thousand of their own drawings. The outputs are lower in resolution and narrower in range. That is the point.

"A big model gives you the average of everyone," says Teodor Halvorsen, who runs a print workshop in Bergen and helped three of the artists set up their pipelines. "A small one gives you the average of you. That's useful, because the average of you is exactly what you want to avoid."
The model shows me my habits. My job is to break them.
Where the hand comes back in

None of the artists exhibit raw outputs. Halvorsen's workshop prints proposals onto cotton paper as faint guides, and the artists draw over, around and against them. In some finished pieces the machine's line survives in a corner. In most it has been erased entirely, leaving only the decision it provoked.

This matters for how the work is credited, and for how it sells. Two of the three galleries we spoke to now ask artists for a short process note listing the tools used and at which stage. Collectors, one dealer said, are less worried about whether a machine was involved than about whether anyone was in charge.

For anyone building a practice around these tools, the studios suggest a working pattern: keep the training data yours, keep the model small enough to understand, and keep the last decision human. Document the process as you go. It becomes part of the work, and part of your record.
Vos puts it more simply. The machine is a boat, she says, and a good one. It still needs someone who knows where they are going.
